summary: Andrew J. Hawkins argues that if the Tesla Cybertruck is deadly to pedestrians, it is mainly because it is a large, heavy, tall-fronted truck, a class of vehicle already known to be dangerous. Little Cybertruck-specific data exists, and neither NHTSA nor IIHS plans crash tests, so experts are waiting for independent data. Questions about its crumple zones, blind spots, and stainless steel body remain unresolved, and the truck is unlikely to be sold in Europe.
one_line: The Cybertruck may be deadly to pedestrians mainly because it is a large truck, but independent crash data is still lacking.
key_facts: The Tesla Cybertruck had been out a little more than a week when the article was published, and it was already being called a safety nightmare.
Neither NHTSA nor IIHS has plans to conduct crash safety tests with the Cybertruck, and it was not on NHTSA's list of vehicles to crash test for 2024.
Last month, an IIHS study confirmed that trucks and SUVs with tall, flat fronts and high hoods are more deadly for pedestrians than more compact vehicles.
Raul Arbelaez, VP of the IIHS Vehicle Research Center, says tall front ends increase risk and a higher point of impact increases risk for cyclists.
Arbelaez says vehicle weight has gone up over the past 20 years and electrification is taking weight increases to another level; EV trucks are heavier due to batteries.
In the US, automakers 'self certify' that vehicles comply with federal safety standards; there is no pre-approval before they can sell cars.
NHTSA's website says the Cybertruck 'meets the performance criteria' for standards like lane departure warnings and dynamic brake support, but it has no five-star safety rating.
Tesla ran its own in-house crash tests, with videos shown at the delivery event, which prompted questions about the truck's crumple zones.
The Cybertruck has steering by wire, removable sideview mirrors, no rearview mirror, and relies on a center console screen to see sides and behind.
Elon Musk is 'highly confident' the Cybertruck will be safer than other trucks for occupants and pedestrians.
All four Tesla vehicles, the Model S, X, 3, and Y, have earned five-star ratings from Euro NCAP.
More people are dying on US roads than at any time in the last 40 years, a crisis tied to vehicle weight, height, and dimensions.
The Cybertruck is unlikely to be sold in Europe; a Tesla lead designer told TopGear Netherlands this, blaming the inflexible stainless steel exterior.
